1	# MergeRadar
2	
3	## One-sentence summary
4	
5	`entire graph merge-radar <a> <b>` finds changes on two agent-built branches
6	that merge cleanly in Git but break each other's assumptions, and explains each
7	conflict in the two agents' own recorded intent from Entire Checkpoints.
8	
9	## Problem, intended user and why it matters
10	
11	Teams now run several coding agents in parallel, each on its own branch or
12	worktree. File isolation stops textual conflicts. It does nothing about logical
13	ones. Agent A changes what a function means; agent B, at the same time, writes
14	new code that calls that function assuming the old meaning. Each branch passes
15	its own tests. Git merges them without a conflict marker. The combined program
16	is wrong, and nobody finds out until it runs.
17	
18	The user is any developer merging agent-built branches, which is now the
19	normal case. The cost is real: the merged code was never executed by anyone,
20	and the failure surfaces after review, when both authors have moved on and
21	neither remembers the assumption that broke.
22	
23	Semantic merge tools can flag the dependency. None of them can say *why* each
24	side made its change, because that reasoning was never recorded before
25	Checkpoints existed.
26	
27	## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
28	
29	Track 2, Build with Graph Intelligence. The track brief lists "combining Entire
30	Graph findings with checkpoint intent" as a direction; this is that.
31	
32	Graph is how the tool connects an entity changed on branch A to code on branch
33	B that consumes it, including through untouched intermediate callers. Remove
34	Graph and the tool is a text diff. Checkpoints are how it explains the
35	collision: what each agent was asked to do and what it believed, quoted from
36	the checkpoint's AI summary or, when no summary exists, from the session's own
37	prompt. Remove Checkpoints and it is a dependency warning with no explanation,
38	which existing tools already give.
39	
40	The two data sources had never been joined. Graph's `checkpoint` command uses
41	a checkpoint ID only to locate a commit; nothing in the plugin opened the
42	transcript or the prompt before this change.
43	
44	## Architecture and main workflow
45	
46	One new subcommand in the Graph plugin, built from pieces that already existed.
47	
48	1. Semantic diff of A against the base and B against the base, using the
49	   existing `AnalyzeGitRange`. Output: entities changed, added or removed on
50	   each side.
51	2. Cross-reference. For every entity changed on A, find entities in B's tree
52	   whose bodies reference it, using the same reference index that powers
53	   `dependents_count` (exported as `sem.ReferencesTo`). A referencing entity
54	   that B also changed or added is a **dependency conflict**. Every referencing
55	   entity is also a candidate for the next hop, so an untouched intermediate
56	   caller still connects a change to new code two hops away (default depth 2,
57	   max 3). Repeated in the other direction. An entity changed on both sides in
58	   the same file is a **direct conflict**.
59	3. Intent. For each commit in base..branch, read the `Entire-Checkpoint`
60	   trailer, resolve `refs/entire/checkpoints/*/<id>`, read the session
61	   `metadata.json` for the AI summary's intent, outcome and open items, and
62	   fall back to `prompt.txt` when no summary exists. The checkpoint whose
63	   `files_touched` includes the conflicting file is chosen; otherwise the
64	   latest with real intent. The report says which.
65	4. Report, text or `--json`, one entry per conflict: the changed entity, the
66	   consumer, the hop chain, both intents with checkpoint id, commit, agent and
67	   source, and a plain-language explanation. Every entry is labelled
68	   `potential` and the report ends with the `git merge-tree --write-tree`
69	   command that produces a merged tree to actually test.
70	
71	Files: `internal/sem/mergeradar.go` (analysis), `internal/sem/mergeradar_intent.go`
72	(checkpoint reading), `internal/gitutil/checkpoint_refs.go` and `merge_base.go`
73	(git plumbing), `internal/cli/mergeradar.go` (command and output), plus one
74	dispatch line in `root.go` and one help entry in `help.go`.
75	
76	Honesty rule carried through the code: the tool never claims breakage it has
77	not observed. A commit without a checkpoint is reported as such, a prompt
78	quoted in place of a summary is labelled, and a truncated quote is marked.
79	
80	## Entire Graph findings and verification
81	
82	- Definition lookup: `entire graph def --repo . --symbol ProviderWarning`
83	  (afternoon, before the curveball edit) returned the struct at
84	  internal/sem/provider.go:278 with Code, Severity, FilePath,
85	  EffectOnCompleteness and Detail. Verified against source: exact. The
86	  coverage block of the revised report is derived from these typed codes,
87	  so no second notion of "could not parse" was invented.
88	- Impact analysis before a risky change: `entire graph impact --repo .
89	  --symbol ReferencesTo|buildReferenceIndex|dependencyConflicts|directConflicts`
90	  before the curveball edit. Reported: ReferencesTo is called by
91	  dependencyConflicts and AnalyzeMerge and wraps buildReferenceIndex, which
92	  has 11 direct callers (ten dependents tests plus ReferencesTo);
93	  dependencyConflicts and directConflicts are reached by runMergeRadar and
94	  five tests and both return MergeConflict. Verified against source: the
95	  chain is exact. Where the graph was incomplete: `--symbol
96	  ConfidencePotential` found nothing (a string constant is not indexed);
97	  the text writer that prints the label (writeMergeConflict) and the "no
98	  conflicts" sentence never appeared as consumers because the graph tracks
99	  call edges, not struct-field reads; and every query printed
100	  "Completeness: degraded" for the graph of this very repository. Both
101	  gaps were consumers the revision had to touch, so the graph's impact
102	  list alone would have been short by two sites.
103	- Final semantic diff: `entire graph diff --repo . --base main --head HEAD`
104	  on the submitted implementation (evidence/final-semantic-diff.txt in the
105	  buildathon folder). It listed 15 files and 205 entity changes: every
106	  function and field added in internal/sem/mergeradar.go (74),
107	  mergeradar_intent.go (25), mergeradar_verify.go (12),
108	  internal/cli/mergeradar.go (20), gitutil/checkpoint_refs.go (13) and the
109	  tests, plus the one-line dispatch change in cli/root.go ("Run body
110	  changed, 564 dependents"). Verified against `git diff --stat main..HEAD`:
111	  the file set matches. Where it was incomplete: help.go appears only as
112	  "module body changed" because the registry is one composite literal, so
113	  the new help entry and its flags are invisible at entity level; DESIGN.md
114	  and .claude/settings.json show as document sections (inventory, not
115	  semantics); and the run carried five E_PARSE_ERROR warnings on vendored
116	  tree-sitter array.h headers, the same partial coverage the curveball
117	  response now reports for its own analysis.
118	
119	## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
120	
121	Constraint received at noon (Track 2, "Graph is evidence, not an oracle"):
122	the product must not present incomplete Graph relationships as certain,
123	must identify when analysis may be partial, must provide a safe fallback
124	or verification path, must keep working for fully resolved code, must
125	include a test or fixture for incomplete analysis, and must let users and
126	agents tell apart structural evidence, heuristic or incomplete evidence,
127	and claims that require source or test verification.
128	
129	**What assumption changed.** Checkpoint 1 decided to reuse the dependents
130	reference index as the answer to "who references this name". That treated
131	every index hit as one kind of evidence, gave every finding the same
132	label, and printed "No cross-branch conflicts found" whenever the index
133	was empty. The card breaks all three: the index matches by short name, so
134	a hit can be a different entity that happens to share a name; interface
135	dispatch, reflection, generated code, prose files and files the parser
136	cannot handle are invisible; and an empty result from a partial analysis
137	is not evidence of safety. We proved this on a real repository before
138	editing: numpy main with two open pull requests (pr-32497 and pr-32510,
139	curveball-fixture/). The pre-curveball build gave 144, 158, 146 and 146
140	findings across four runs of the same command, 60 of them hops through
141	.rst documents by words like "array" and "less", 40 with one end in a C
142	file that failed to parse, and 772 warnings printed after every finding.
143	The fresh session reconstructed the work from checkpoints b1b09589d199
144	and 17790384bf09, then ran `entire graph impact` on ReferencesTo,
145	buildReferenceIndex, dependencyConflicts and directConflicts before any
146	edit (see the findings above for where the graph was right and where it
147	was short).
148	
149	**How the design changed.** The pipeline, the intent reader and the report
150	shape are unchanged; four additive things were built, tests first. (1)
151	Every finding carries an evidence class: structural when each hop
152	resolved to exactly one parsed entity, heuristic when the matched short
153	name has several definitions at the consumer head, a hop is a method
154	(possible dynamic dispatch) or a document, or a provider warning touches
155	a file in the chain, with a note saying which. Confidence stays
156	"potential" for both. (2) The report opens with its coverage: complete,
157	or partial with a one-line summary and the reasons, derived from the
158	graph's own typed warnings (E_PARSE_ERROR, W_UNSUPPORTED_FILE and the
159	rest, counted by code and by changed files affected), ambiguous names,
160	"Code generated" headers and reflect imports. When nothing is found under
161	partial coverage the text says "No conflicts found, but analysis is
162	partial:" and never the plain sentence. (3) `--verify` builds the merged
163	tree with `git merge-tree --write-tree`, checks it out in a temporary
164	worktree and runs the repository's tests (Go modules today), recording
165	reproduced with the failing output, passed (still potential), conflicted
166	when git itself cannot merge, or unavailable with the manual commands.
167	(4) The walk visits names in sorted order so the count is deterministic,
168	document entities are excluded unless `--include-docs`, and identical
169	files on both branches are not reported as direct conflicts. Tests:
170	TestAnalyzeMergeMarksAmbiguousNameHeuristic,
171	TestAnalyzeMergeReportsPartialAnalysis,
172	TestAnalyzeMergeMarksUnparsedFileHeuristic,
173	TestAnalyzeMergeIsDeterministicWhenTwoOriginsShareAHop,
174	TestAnalyzeMergeSkipsDocumentsUnlessIncluded,
175	TestAnalyzeMergeIgnoresIdenticalChangesOnBothSides,
176	TestVerifyMergeReproducesTheBreak, TestVerifyMergePassesWhenTestsStillPass,
177	TestVerifyMergeUnavailableWithoutRunner and
178	TestWriteMergeRadarTextStatesEvidenceAndCoverage; the existing dependency
179	test now also asserts its finding is structural, which is the proof that
180	fully resolved code behaves as before.
181	
182	**Why the new result is safe.** The same numpy command now opens with
183	"analysis PARTIAL: 229 file(s) failed to parse, 5 unsupported, 18
184	ambiguous name(s); 5 changed file(s) affected" and names the PRs' own C
185	files that did not parse, before any finding is read; the count is the
186	same on every run (57: 2 structural, 55 heuristic; the 20 direct "conflicts"
187	the old build reported on files pr-32510 shares byte for byte with pr-32497
188	are gone), every heuristic
189	finding says why ("ambiguous name: 3 definitions of dispatcher",
190	"file did not parse: abstractdtypes.c"), and no finding passes through a
191	document. `--verify` on that pair reports "verification conflicted": git
192	itself cannot merge the two PRs (add/add on two release-note files), a
193	fact the old report never mentioned, and prints the manual path. On the
194	demo fixture the report stays "analysis complete" with two structural
195	findings and `--verify` reproduces the break: "expected 2.00 rupees, got
196	0.02". A reader can now tell apart what the graph proved, what it guessed,
197	and what only a test run can settle, and the tool never says "safe" when
198	it did not look. BEFORE and AFTER outputs are saved side by side in
199	curveball-fixture/.
200	
201	## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
202	
203	Fork: https://github.com/Piyush-Goenka/entire-graph (branch merge-radar).
204	Open any checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain <id>` in the clone; each
205	carries an AI summary and the session transcript behind the commit.
206	
207	1. Initial understanding and intended architecture: checkpoint ea7a792286b0,
208	   commit 95b4c08 (https://github.com/Piyush-Goenka/entire-graph/commit/95b4c08).
209	   Proves the design, the rejected alternatives and the assumption ("reuse
210	   the dependents reference index") that the curveball later invalidated.
211	2. Last stable state before noon: checkpoint 17790384bf09, commit 6ffa8ef
212	   (https://github.com/Piyush-Goenka/entire-graph/commit/6ffa8ef). Proves
213	   steps 1 to 4 working end to end with tests, and names the open risk
214	   (reproduction printed, not run). Commits 909ab25, c65cacb, 1ff4ba1 and
215	   7999626 carry the intermediate checkpoints.
216	3. Response to the Noon Curveball: checkpoint 431773deb4dc, commit 1390a5e
217	   (https://github.com/Piyush-Goenka/entire-graph/commit/1390a5e). Built
218	   from the fresh session's transcript, so it contains the reconstruction
219	   from checkpoints, the impact analysis run before editing, the tests
220	   written first, and the numpy BEFORE and AFTER runs.
221	4. Final implementation and verification: the tip of merge-radar
222	   (https://github.com/Piyush-Goenka/entire-graph/commits/merge-radar), the
223	   SHA given in the submission. Adds this document and demo/ to the fork and
224	   records the final semantic diff.
225	
226	## Setup, run and test instructions
227	
228	```
229	git clone <fork>
230	cd entire-graph
231	go build -o entire-graph ./cmd/entire-graph          # Go 1.26 (toolchain auto-downloads)
232	go test ./internal/sem -run 'AnalyzeMerge|CheckpointIntents|TruncateRunes|Verify|DescribeRefs'
233	go test ./internal/cli -run 'MergeRadar|Registry|EveryCommandDoc'
234	go test ./internal/gitutil
235	```
236	
237	Demo repository (two branches, two agents, checkpoints):
238	
239	```
240	demo/make-fixture.sh /tmp/radar-demo --fake-checkpoints   # offline fixture, labelled synthetic
241	./entire-graph merge-radar pricing-rupees invoicing --repo /tmp/radar-demo
242	./entire-graph merge-radar pricing-rupees invoicing --repo /tmp/radar-demo --json
243	./entire-graph merge-radar pricing-rupees invoicing --repo /tmp/radar-demo --verify   # runs the merged tree's tests
244	demo/make-fixture.sh /tmp/radar-demo --prove              # both branches pass alone; merged tree fails
245	
246	Curveball fixture (numpy, two real pull requests; each run takes about two minutes):
247	
248	```
249	cd curveball-fixture/numpy
250	entire graph merge-radar pr-32497 pr-32510 --repo .            # AFTER output: curveball-fixture/after-merge-radar.txt
251	entire graph merge-radar pr-32497 pr-32510 --repo . --verify   # git cannot merge the pair: "verification conflicted"
252	```
253	```
254	
255	As an installed plugin the same command is `entire graph merge-radar ...`.
256	
257	## Databricks use, data sources and limitations
258	
259	Not entered.
260	
261	## Known limitations and next steps
262	
263	One language exercised end to end (Go); the reference index is language-agnostic
264	in principle but only Go was tested today. Conflicts expressed through
265	configuration, serialised data or runtime strings are invisible to the graph and
266	the report says so. Intent quality depends on checkpoints existing on the
267	branch; a branch without them gets a dependency warning with no explanation,
268	clearly labelled. Depth is bounded. `--verify` runs the merged tree's tests only
269	for Go modules; other ecosystems get "verification unavailable" and the manual
270	commands, never an implied pass. The evidence class is a conservative rule
271	(ambiguous name, method, document or unparsed file in the chain), so a real
272	break can be labelled heuristic; heuristic never means ignored, only "the graph
273	could not prove this, run the tests". The coverage block reports what the parser
274	and the reference walk could not see; it cannot report what it never knew to
275	look for, such as a call built from a string at runtime.
276	
277	Next step toward production: run as a check on pull requests targeting the same
278	base so the report appears before a human reviews the merge, add test runners
279	for the other ecosystems (pytest, npm test, cargo test) so `--verify` can
280	upgrade `potential` to `reproduced` beyond Go.

Both files read. Here is the five-sentence statement for checkpoint 4.

The submitted command, `entire graph merge-radar <a> <b>`, finds changes on two agent-built branches that merge cleanly in Git but break each other, labels each finding with the evidence class the graph could actually establish (structural or heuristic, with the reason), opens with its own coverage (complete or partial), explains each collision in both agents' recorded checkpoint intent, and with `--verify` builds the merged tree with `git merge-tree` and runs its tests. The final semantic diff (`entire graph diff --base main --head HEAD`, saved as evidence/final-semantic-diff.txt and .json) listed 15 files and 205 entity changes covering every function and field added in mergeradar.go, mergeradar_intent.go, mergeradar_verify.go, cli/mergeradar.go, checkpoint_refs.go and their tests, plus the one-line dispatch change in root.go ("Run body changed, 564 dependents") and matched `git diff --stat main..HEAD` file for file, but the graph was incomplete where help.go and help_test.go appeared only as "module body changed" because the help registry is one composite literal (so the new entry and its flags are invisible at entity level), where DESIGN.md and .claude/settings.json showed as document sections rather than semantics, and where the run itself carried five E_PARSE_ERROR warnings on vendored tree-sitter array.h headers. Verification was: `go test ./internal/sem` (full package, 389 s), `./internal/cli` and `./internal/gitutil` all passing at checkpoint 3's tree with the merge-radar test set passing in about 30 s and a clean-checkout build succeeding; a demo with two live Claude Code agents on disjoint files where each branch was green alone, the merge was clean, the merged tests failed, and merge-radar explained why in the agents' own checkpoint summaries and reproduced the failure with `--verify` ("expected 2.00 rupees, got 0.02"); and a real-repository check on numpy with two open pull requests where the report opens with "analysis PARTIAL", gives a deterministic 57 findings (2 structural, 55 heuristic) instead of the old 144 to 158, and `--verify` correctly reports "verification conflicted" because git itself cannot merge the pair. Four checkpoints exist: ea7a792286b0 (commit 95b4c08) proves the design, rejected alternatives and the "reuse the dependents reference index" assumption the curveball later invalidated; 17790384bf09 (commit 6ffa8ef) proves the pre-noon pipeline working end to end with tests and names the open risk that reproduction was printed, not run; 431773deb4dc (commit 1390a5e) proves the curveball response, built from the fresh session that reconstructed the work from checkpoints, ran `entire graph impact` before editing, wrote tests first and captured the numpy BEFORE and AFTER runs; and checkpoint 4, the tip of merge-radar, adds BUILDATHON.md and demo/ with no code changes and records the final semantic diff. The known limitations, stated honestly, are that only one language (Go) was exercised end to end, `--verify` runs tests only for Go modules and reports "unavailable" elsewhere rather than an implied pass, the evidence rule is conservative so a real break can be labelled heuristic, conflicts expressed through configuration, serialised data or runtime strings are invisible, intent quality depends on checkpoints existing on the branch, and the coverage block reports what the parser and walk could not see but never what they did not know to look for.
